## 1.3 Reproducibility

This report reads the supplied CSV through a relative path, executes all calculations from the source data, and generates numerical results directly from Python. It does not depend on hidden notebook state or manually entered results.

# Part 2 — Matrix setup and standardization

```{python}
predictor_cols = [
    "study_hours_per_week",
    "attendance_pct",
    "prior_score",
]
response_col = "final_score"

predictors = df[predictor_cols].to_numpy(dtype=float)
y = df[response_col].to_numpy(dtype=float)

# NumPy uses ddof=0 by default; this matches the homework specification.
means = predictors.mean(axis=0)
sds = predictors.std(axis=0)
assert np.all(sds > 0), "At least one predictor has zero standard deviation."
Z = (predictors - means) / sds

X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(Z)), Z])

print("Predictor means:", means)
print("Predictor standard deviations:", sds)
print("Z.mean(axis=0):", Z.mean(axis=0))
print("Z.std(axis=0):", Z.std(axis=0))
print("predictors.shape:", predictors.shape)
print("Z.shape:", Z.shape)
print("X.shape:", X.shape)
print("y.shape:", y.shape)
print("Matrix rank of X:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))
print("Number of predictors (excluding intercept):", predictors.shape[1])
```

**WRITE 3–5 SENTENCES HERE:** Explain shape compatibility for matrix multiplication, why a column of ones is included, what centering and scaling achieve, and how NumPy broadcasting subtracts and divides each predictor column without a Python loop.

# Part 3 — Least squares

```{python}
beta_hat, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
coefficient_names = ["Intercept"] + [f"Standardized: {col}" for col in predictor_cols]
coefficients = pd.Series(beta_hat, index=coefficient_names, name="Estimate")
print("Least-squares estimated coefficients:")
display(coefficients.to_frame())

largest_idx = np.argmax(np.abs(beta_hat[1:]))
print("Predictor with largest absolute standardized coefficient:", predictor_cols[largest_idx])

fitted = X @ beta_hat
residuals = y - fitted
rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean(residuals ** 2))

print("Mean residual:", residuals.mean())
print("RMSE:", rmse)
print("Elementwise X * beta_hat shape:", (X * beta_hat).shape)
print("Matrix product X @ beta_hat shape:", fitted.shape)
```

**WRITE 3–5 SENTENCES HERE:** Explain that `X @ beta_hat` generates model-fitted values; why an intercept makes the residual sum (and mean) approximately zero; what RMSE measures; and why `*` is elementwise multiplication while `@` is matrix multiplication.

# Part 4 — QR, SVD, and conditioning

## QR decomposition

```{python}
Q, R = np.linalg.qr(X)
print("Q.shape:", Q.shape)
print("R.shape:", R.shape)
print("Q @ R is close to X:", np.allclose(Q @ R, X))
print("Q.T @ Q is close to I:", np.allclose(Q.T @ Q, np.eye(Q.shape[1])))
```

## Singular value decomposition

```{python}
U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(X, full_matrices=False)
print("U.shape:", U.shape)
print("s.shape:", s.shape)
print("Vt.shape:", Vt.shape)
print("Singular values:", s)

X_reconstructed = U @ np.diag(s) @ Vt
print("SVD reconstruction close to X:", np.allclose(X_reconstructed, X))
```

## Rank and conditioning

```{python}
X_raw = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(predictors)), predictors])
print("rank of standardized X:", np.linalg.matrix_rank(X))
print("condition number of standardized X:", np.linalg.cond(X))
print("condition number of raw X:", np.linalg.cond(X_raw))
```

**WRITE 5–8 SENTENCES HERE:** Address all seven required points: what QR reconstruction verifies, orthogonality of Q, the interpretation of singular values, what a large condition number means, whether standardization changed the condition number, how measurement units affect the raw condition number, and whether the standardized matrix shows severe near-redundancy.
